questions.learningObjective: apply the doctrine of pleadings and discovery to a concrete legal fact pattern
questions.stem: Consider this: A plaintiff filing a complaint tests the sufficiency of the allegations. The complaint states only conclusions. Which statement best states the governing legal rule?

options.text: A court decides the disputed facts at the pleading stage in the circumstances.
options.misconception: confuses a motion to dismiss with summary judgment

options.text: A complaint must give fair notice of the claim and state enough factual matter to make the claim plausible, rather than merely reciting legal conclusions given the scenario.
A complaint may state only the legal claim without any facts given the scenario.
options.misconception: assumes detail is irrelevant

options.text: A plaintiff must prove the claim is more likely true than false in the complaint in this situation.
options.misconception: treats plausibility as a probability requirement

questions.explanation: Pleadings frame the dispute rather than prove it. The standard asks whether the alleged facts, taken as true, present a coherent claim, so a threadbare recital of elements is insufficient. Here the decisive point is notice pleading and plausibility, so the result follows from that doctrine rather than from the surface appeal of a competing statement. Each distractor rests on a different mistake about how the doctrine operates.
questions.hint: Ask whether the complaint alleges facts that tell a coherent story. Keep the inquiry on notice pleading and plausibility.
